props.title: Cleopatra
props.initialSlug: Power and passion ignite an empire

sections.content: Cleopatra stands as one of Hollywood's most infamous epic productions, nearly bankrupting 20th Century Fox with its $31 million budget (equivalent to $280 million today). Elizabeth Taylor's portrayal of the Egyptian queen redefined screen glamour, with her 65 costume changes and iconic entrance into Rome becoming cinema legend. The film's troubled production, including Taylor's near-fatal illness and the scandalous Taylor-Burton affair that began on set, overshadowed Joseph L. Mankiewicz's ambitious 6-hour vision, eventually cut to 4 hours. This massive undertaking followed the tradition of biblical epics like The Ten Commandments (1956) and Ben-Hur (1959), but with unprecedented scale.

sections.content: The historical epic genre peaked in the 1950s and early 1960s, with films like Quo Vadis (1951) and The Fall of the Roman Empire (1964) showcasing massive sets, thousands of extras, and meticulous attention to period detail. These productions represented Hollywood's attempt to combat television's growing popularity by offering spectacular entertainment impossible to replicate on the small screen. Cleopatra's lavish production design, particularly the Alexandria and Rome sequences, set new standards for historical accuracy in set decoration and costume design.

The film's influence extends beyond its era, inspiring later historical epics like Gladiator (2000) and Alexander (2004). Modern CGI-enhanced productions still reference Cleopatra's practical effects achievements, particularly its massive crowd scenes and detailed recreations of ancient cities. The film's handling of political intrigue and power dynamics between Cleopatra, Julius Caesar, and Mark Antony continues to influence contemporary historical dramas. sections.content: Cleopatra's influence on cinematic portrayals of ancient Egypt remains unmatched. Later films like The Mummy (1999) and Exodus: Gods and Kings (2014) drew from its visual vocabulary of ancient Egyptian imagery. The film's elaborate makeup techniques, particularly Taylor's iconic eye makeup, created a template for depicting ancient Egyptian royalty that persists in popular culture. Despite its initial financial failure, Cleopatra pioneered numerous filmmaking techniques and set decoration methods still studied today.
